alt: Three plan views. Dispersed: isolated farmhouses spread across fields, typical of large or pastoral farms where water is everywhere. Nucleated: houses clustered round a crossroads or well, for shared water, defence or cooperation. Linear: houses in a line along a road, also found along railways, rivers, coasts and valley floors.
caption: Name the pattern, then give a reason tied to a feature you can see.

alt: A schematic landscape with six numbered settlements: 1 on a dry point above a marshy floodplain; 2 inside a meander loop for defence, like Durham; 3 at a bridging point; 4 at a spring, a wet point; 5 in a gap through the hills; 6 on a sheltered, sunny slope. A key below names each site factor.
caption: Early sites met basic needs: water, safety from floods and attack, crossings and routes.

after: ## Key idea 4: the hierarchy of settlements and services
alt: A stepped pyramid from isolated dwelling at the base through hamlet, village, town and city to conurbation at the top. An arrow upwards notes fewer settlements, each larger and further apart, with more and higher-order services and a larger sphere of influence. Below, threshold and range explain why only large settlements support high-order services.
caption: Threshold and range decide which services each level can support.

after: ## Key idea 4: the hierarchy of settlements and services
alt: Causes of rural service closure (more car ownership, online shopping and banking, ageing or declining population) lead to the loss of village shops, banks and post offices. Responses include mobile libraries, clinics and banking vans, multi-purpose shops with a post office and café, and community-run shops. In fast-growing cities the problem is the reverse.
caption: Fewer local customers push services away; mobile and shared services fill the gap.

after: ## Worked example: measuring a sphere of influence
alt: Three circles centred on a market town show the spheres of influence of a newsagent (furthest customer 4 km), a supermarket (15 km) and a furniture store (55 km), with desire lines to customers’ homes. A table gives mean and furthest distances: newsagent 1.5 and 4 km, supermarket 6 and 15 km, furniture store 22 and 55 km. The furniture store is high-order; the newsagent low-order.
caption: High-order services draw customers from much further away.
